source_refs.note: Book p. 35-36: derivative of sin x by definition, Try yourself! box, derivatives of the other trigonometric functions, Example 1, box of six trigonometric derivatives, Example 2

blocks.text:
While finding derivatives of trigonometric functions, we assume that the angle is measured in radians. To calculate the derivative of \(f(x) = \sin x\).
Here, \(f(x + h) = \sin(x + h)\), and
\[f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}\]
(By the definition of derivative)
\[= \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{\sin(x+h) - \sin x}{h}\]
(By substituting the values)
Using \(\sin p - \sin q = 2\cos\frac{p+q}{2}\sin\frac{p-q}{2}\) with \(p = x + h\), \(q = x\):
\[\dfrac{p+q}{2} = \dfrac{x+h+x}{2} = \dfrac{2x+h}{2}\]
\[\dfrac{p-q}{2} = \dfrac{x+h-x}{2} = \dfrac{h}{2}\]
\[f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{2\cos\left(\frac{2x+h}{2}\right)\sin\left(\frac{h}{2}\right)}{h}\]
Applying the limit \(h \to 0\):
\[= \lim_{h \to 0}\cos\left(\dfrac{2x+h}{2}\right)\]
\[\quad \cdot \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{\sin(h/2)}{h/2}\]
\[= \cos x\,(1) = \cos x\]
\(\left(\because \lim_{\theta \to 0}\frac{\sin\theta}{\theta} = 1,\ \theta \text{ is measured in radians}\right)\)
Thus \(\frac{d}{dx}(\sin x) = \cos x\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
What happened in each line: we wrote the definition, substituted sin, changed the difference of two sines into a product (so that a factor \(\sin(h/2)\) appears), and arranged \(\frac{\sin(h/2)}{h/2}\), whose limit is 1.
Why \(\frac{h}{2}\) in the denominator: \(\frac{2\sin(h/2)}{h} = \frac{\sin(h/2)}{h/2}\). The 2 in front was used to turn \(h\) into \(h/2\), so the standard limit with \(\theta = h/2\) can be applied.
Why radians: the limit \(\lim_{\theta \to 0}\frac{\sin\theta}{\theta} = 1\) is true only when \(\theta\) is in radians. In degrees the limit is \(\frac{\pi}{180}\), and every trigonometric derivative would carry that extra factor.

blocks.title: The derivative of the sine function is the cosine function
Teaching note
blocks.text:
A guide for the Try yourself! box (follow the same steps as for sine):
Use \(\cos p - \cos q = -2\sin\frac{p+q}{2}\sin\frac{p-q}{2}\) with \(p = x + h\), \(q = x\):
\[\dfrac{\cos(x+h) - \cos x}{h}\]
\[= \dfrac{-2\sin\left(\frac{2x+h}{2}\right)\sin\left(\frac{h}{2}\right)}{h}\]
\[= -\sin\left(\dfrac{2x+h}{2}\right) \cdot \dfrac{\sin(h/2)}{h/2}\]
Let \(h \to 0\): the first factor tends to \(\sin x\) and the second to 1, so
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}(\cos x) = -\sin x\]
Derivative of the Other Trigonometric Functions
After finding derivatives of \(\sin x\) and \(\cos x\) by definition, the derivatives of the remaining trigonometric functions can be found using product rule and quotient rule of differentiation.

blocks.title: Example 1
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = \tan x\).
To find: \(f'(x)\).
Method: write \(\tan x = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}\) and use the quotient rule, together with the derivatives of \(\sin x\) and \(\cos x\) that were found by definition.

Step 1: Write tan x as a quotient
\[f(x) = \tan x = \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\]
Why: we already know the derivatives of \(\sin x\) and \(\cos x\); the quotient rule \(\left(\frac{u}{v}\right)' = \frac{u'v - uv'}{v^{2}}\) joins them, with \(u = \sin x\), \(v = \cos x\).

Step 2: Apply the quotient rule (differentiating w.r.t. x)
\[u'v = (\sin x)'\cos x = \cos x\cos x\]
\[uv' = \sin x(\cos x)' = \sin x(-\sin x)\]
\[f'(x) = \dfrac{\cos x\cos x - \sin x(-\sin x)}{\cos^{2} x}\]
Why: \((\sin x)' = \cos x\) and \((\cos x)' = -\sin x\).

Step 3: Simplify
\[f'(x) = \dfrac{\cos^{2} x + \sin^{2} x}{\cos^{2} x}\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{\cos^{2} x} = \sec^{2} x\]
Why: minus times minus is plus; \(\sin^{2} x + \cos^{2} x = 1\); and \(\frac{1}{\cos x} = \sec x\).
Check: at \(x = \frac{\pi}{4}\) the formula gives \(\sec^{2}\frac{\pi}{4} = 2\). Numerically, \(\frac{\tan(0.7864) - \tan(0.7844)}{0.002} \approx 2.000\). The slopes agree.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book labels Example 1 "(By using definition)", but the solution does not use the limit definition of the derivative directly: it uses the quotient rule together with \((\sin x)' = \cos x\) and \((\cos x)' = -\sin x\) (which were found by definition). The label should read "(By using the quotient rule)". The result \(\frac{d}{dx}(\tan x) = \sec^{2} x\) is correct.

blocks.title: The Derivatives of Six Trigonometric Functions
blocks.text:
(i) \(\frac{d}{dx}(\sin x) = \cos x\)
(ii) \(\frac{d}{dx}(\cos x) = -\sin x\)
(iii) \(\frac{d}{dx}(\tan x) = \sec^{2} x\)
(iv) \(\frac{d}{dx}(\cot x) = -\csc^{2} x\)
(v) \(\frac{d}{dx}(\sec x) = \sec x\tan x\)
(vi) \(\frac{d}{dx}(\csc x) = \csc x\cot x\)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
Formula (vi) is printed as \(\frac{d}{dx}(\csc x) = \csc x\cot x\). The correct formula has a minus sign:
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}(\csc x) = -\csc x\cot x\]
Proof: \(\csc x = \frac{1}{\sin x}\), so by the quotient rule \((\csc x)' = \frac{0 \cdot \sin x - 1 \cdot \cos x}{\sin^{2} x} = -\frac{1}{\sin x}\cdot\frac{\cos x}{\sin x} = -\csc x\cot x\). The book itself uses the minus sign in Example 2.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The other three formulas come the same way from the quotient rule:
\(\sec x = \frac{1}{\cos x}\): \((\sec x)' = \frac{0 - 1(-\sin x)}{\cos^{2} x} = \frac{1}{\cos x}\cdot\frac{\sin x}{\cos x} = \sec x\tan x\).
\(\cot x = \frac{\cos x}{\sin x}\): \((\cot x)' = \frac{-\sin^{2} x - \cos^{2} x}{\sin^{2} x} = -\frac{1}{\sin^{2} x} = -\csc^{2} x\).
Memory aid: the derivatives of the 'co' functions (\(\cos\), \(\cot\), \(\csc\)) all carry a minus sign. Each co-formula is the plain formula with every function replaced by its co-function and a minus sign added: \(\tan \to \sec^{2}\) gives \(\cot \to -\csc^{2}\); \(\sec \to \sec\tan\) gives \(\csc \to -\csc\cot\).

blocks.title: Example 2
steps:
Given: \(y = x^{2}\csc x\).
To find: \(\frac{dy}{dx}\).
Method: \(y\) is a product of \(u = x^{2}\) and \(v = \csc x\), so use the product rule with \((\csc x)' = -\csc x\cot x\).

Step 1: Product rule (differentiating w.r.t. x)
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = (x^{2})'\csc x + x^{2}(\csc x)'\]
Why: \((uv)' = u'v + uv'\).

Step 2: Put in the derivatives
\[= 2x\csc x + x^{2}(-\csc x\cot x)\]
\[= 2x\csc x - x^{2}\csc x\cot x\]
Why: power rule gives \((x^{2})' = 2x\); formula (vi), with its correct minus sign, gives \((\csc x)' = -\csc x\cot x\).

Step 3: Take out the common factor
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = x\csc x\,(2 - x\cot x)\]
Why: both terms contain \(x\csc x\).

Check: multiply out: \(x\csc x \cdot 2 - x\csc x \cdot x\cot x = 2x\csc x - x^{2}\csc x\cot x\), the line of Step 2. Note that the book's own solution uses the minus sign, which confirms the correction to box (vi).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Our examples:
(a) \(\frac{d}{dx}(x\sin x) = (1)\sin x + x\cos x = \sin x + x\cos x\) (product rule).
(b) \(\frac{d}{dx}(3\tan x - 2\sec x) = 3\sec^{2} x - 2\sec x\tan x\) (constant multiple and difference rules).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Angles are in radians; the derivative of \(\sin x\) by definition rests on \(\lim_{\theta \to 0}\frac{\sin\theta}{\theta} = 1\).
2. \((\sin x)' = \cos x\), \((\cos x)' = -\sin x\); the other four follow by the quotient rule.
3. \((\tan x)' = \sec^{2} x\), \((\cot x)' = -\csc^{2} x\), \((\sec x)' = \sec x\tan x\), \((\csc x)' = -\csc x\cot x\).
4. The co-functions (cos, cot, csc) have a minus sign in their derivatives.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Writing \((\cos x)' = \sin x\) or \((\csc x)' = \csc x\cot x\): the minus sign is missing.
2. Using degrees: the formulas hold only for \(x\) in radians.
3. Writing \((\tan x)' = \sec x\): it is \(\sec^{2} x\).
4. Writing \((x^{2}\csc x)' = 2x(-\csc x\cot x)\): a product needs the product rule, not two derivatives multiplied.
